subject: physics
title: The gas laws and the ideal gas equation
key_idea: The gas laws link pressure, volume and temperature for a fixed mass of gas, and combine into pV = nRT or pV = NkT. Temperature must be in kelvin. An ideal gas obeys these equations at all pressures and temperatures.

blocks.text: Gas calculations count particles in moles. This section covers the mole, the Avogadro constant and molar mass.

items.meaning: The amount of substance containing the same number of particles as there are atoms in 12 g of carbon-12. Amount of substance is an SI base quantity, with unit mol.
The number of particles in one mole: 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
The mass of one mole of a substance, in kg mol⁻¹ or g mol⁻¹.
The mass of one molecule: m = M / N_A.

blocks.label: Number of particles
where: N is the number of particles
n is the amount of substance (mol)

blocks.text: One mole of any substance contains N_A particles of that substance.

items: One mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles.
Molar mass is per mole; molecular mass is per molecule.

blocks.text: The gas laws are experimental relationships between pressure p, volume V, thermodynamic temperature T and the mass of the gas.

items: Temperature T must be in **kelvin** for these relationships to hold.
Together they give pV ∝ T for a fixed mass of gas.
A gas that obeys pV ∝ T at all pressures and temperatures is called an **ideal gas**.
A graph of pressure against temperature in °C is a straight line. Extended back, it meets the temperature axis at about −273 °C. This leads to the idea of **absolute zero**.

diagram.alt: Pressure against temperature in degrees Celsius for a fixed volume of gas. A straight line that, extended backwards, reaches zero pressure at about minus 273 degrees Celsius.

items: Boyle: pV constant. Charles: V / T constant. Pressure law: p / T constant.
Use kelvin, and keep the mass of gas fixed.
Extending a p–θ graph back to zero pressure gives absolute zero.

blocks.text: The three laws combine into one equation of state. It links the pressure, volume and temperature of a gas to the amount of gas.

blocks.label: Equation of state (moles)
where: n is the amount of gas (mol)
R is the molar gas constant, 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

blocks.label: Equation of state (molecules)
where: N is the number of molecules
k is the Boltzmann constant, 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹

blocks.label: The Boltzmann constant
where: k is the gas constant per molecule (J K⁻¹)
R is the molar gas constant (J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)

blocks.text: The two forms agree because N = nN_A, so NkT = nN_A × (R / N_A) × T = nRT.

diagram.alt: A slider that changes the amount of gas, its temperature and its volume to show the pressure from the ideal gas equation.

items: pV = nRT and pV = NkT describe an ideal gas.
Use pascals, cubic metres and kelvin in the equation.
k = R / N_A links the two forms.

checks.q: A sample contains 0.25 mol of helium. Calculate the number of atoms in the sample. The Avogadro constant is 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
A gas at 300 K and a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa occupies 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Calculate the amount of gas in moles. R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
A fixed volume of gas is heated from 300 K to 450 K. Its initial pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Calculate the final pressure.
checks.a: p / T is constant, so p = 1.0 × 10⁵ × 450 / 300 = 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa.

items: The work done by a gas expanding at constant pressure is pΔV.
Boyle's law: trap a fixed mass of air in a sealed tube above oil. Change the pressure with a pump and read it from a gauge.
Read the volume from the length of the air column. Wait each time for the temperature to settle.
A graph of p against 1 / V is a straight line through the origin.
Charles's law: trap a column of air in a capillary tube with a drop of acid, and put it in a water bath of known temperature.
Read the length of the air column as the water temperature changes. Keep the whole column under water and stir the bath.
A graph of length against temperature in °C is a straight line. Extended back, it meets the temperature axis at about −273 °C.
Boyle's law: change the volume of a fixed mass of gas and read the pressure. Check that pV is constant.
Pressure law: keep a fixed volume of gas in a flask in a water bath, with a pressure gauge.
Record the pressure at several temperatures and wait for the gas to reach each temperature.
Plot pressure against temperature in °C. Extend the line back to zero pressure to estimate absolute zero.

blocks.text: The estimate comes out close to −273 °C. The extended line is an extrapolation, because a real gas liquefies before it reaches that temperature.
